passage: Class teacher's note, Class 5. Amandeep and Jeevan have been inseparable since Class 1. This week a new boy, Farhan, joined and sits next to Jeevan in maths. Today at lunch Amandeep sat at the far end of the bench, not eating. When Jeevan laughed at something Farhan said, Amandeep said loudly, "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat." Later he tore a page in his notebook and said it was an accident. I spoke with him quietly. He said, "Jeevan will forget me." I have paired all three for next week's science model.

qa.q: Where does Farhan sit in maths?
qa.a: He sits next to Jeevan.

qa.q: What was Amandeep afraid of, based on what he told the teacher?
qa.a: That Jeevan would forget him and choose the new boy as his friend instead.

qa.q: Why is pairing all three for the science model a sensible step?
qa.a: It lets Amandeep see he can share Jeevan without losing him, and gives him a chance to know Farhan.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel hearing "He's only nice to you because you have the new bat"?
qa.a: Hurt and unwelcome, since he is new and the remark says his friendship isn't real.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a boy's fear of losing his best friend to a newcomer.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Ma'am gave the Annual Day solo to the new girl, Kirti. I've sung the solo for three years. Everyone clapped for her at practice, even Mridul, who always says my voice is the best. I clapped too, but my hands felt stiff. At lunch Mridul sat with her to ask how she learned. I stayed in the classroom pretending to finish homework. What if everyone likes her more now? What if Mridul does? I know Kirti didn't do anything wrong. That makes it worse, somehow. 😔
- Himani

qa.q: What did Ma'am give to Kirti?
qa.a: The Annual Day solo.

qa.q: What was Himani afraid of when Mridul sat with Kirti?
qa.a: Himani feared losing the spot as the best singer and losing Mridul's attention to the new girl.

qa.q: What small step could help Himani with this feeling?
qa.a: Talking to Mridul or a trusted adult about the feeling, and perhaps asking Ma'am about another part to sing.

qa.q: How might Kirti experience the class?
qa.a: As a new girl she may simply feel relieved to be welcomed, unaware that Himani is hurting.

grounding: It shows a child afraid of losing both her status as the singer and a friend's attention to a new rival.

passage: In the village, Sahil and Vijay had grazed the goats together every evening since they were small. Then Kamlesh's cousin came from the city for the summer with a real leather football, and Vijay started going to the school ground instead. On the third evening, Sahil walked the goats alone past the ground. He could hear Vijay shouting, "Pass! Pass!" Sahil didn't look. He whacked a bush with his stick harder than he needed to. At home he told his mother the goats were slow today, and he went to bed without eating his rotis.

qa.q: What did the city cousin bring?
qa.a: A real leather football.

qa.q: Why did Sahil whack the bush harder than he needed to?
qa.a: He was hurt that Vijay was choosing the city boy's game over their evenings together, and the feeling came out through his arm.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil to do?
qa.a: Tell Vijay he misses their evenings, or go to the ground and ask to join, instead of staying away alone.

qa.q: What might Vijay not realise about Sahil?
qa.a: He may be enjoying the new football and not notice that Sahil feels left behind.

grounding: It shows a village boy's fear of losing his friend to a newcomer with something exciting to offer.

passage: Every afternoon in Durban, Zanele and Jin walked home together, sharing a packet of chips. Then a new girl joined their class and sat next to Jin. On Tuesday, Jin laughed at something the new girl said, a real, loud laugh. Zanele's chest went tight. At the gate she said, 'Are you walking with me or her?' Jin blinked. 'Both of you?' Zanele kicked a stone and walked ahead. At home she lay on her bed, thinking: what if Jin likes her better? What if I end up walking alone?

qa.q: What did Zanele and Jin share on their walk home?
qa.a: They shared a packet of chips.

qa.q: What was Zanele afraid of when her chest went tight?
qa.a: She feared losing Jin's friendship and attention to the new girl.

qa.q: What could Zanele try instead of walking ahead?
qa.a: She could walk with both of them and tell Jin later that she felt worried, since Jin seemed happy to include her.

qa.q: How might Jin see Zanele's question at the gate?
qa.a: Jin seems confused, not realising Zanele felt threatened, since Jin assumed all three could walk together.

grounding: Illustrates a child's jealous fear of losing a friend to a new peer, set in South Africa.

passage: At the Saturday dance class in the community centre, Vidya had always stood in the front row. This week the teacher moved a new boy, Jagdish, to the front and gave him the short solo. Vidya smiled stiffly and moved to the side. During the break she watched the teacher help Jagdish with his hand movements. Vidya practised her steps in the corner, faster and harder than needed. When the teacher called, 'Vidya, good energy!' she didn't answer. On the way out she asked her mother, 'Do you think Ma'am likes him more now?'

qa.q: What did the teacher give Jagdish this week?
qa.a: She moved him to the front and gave him the short solo.

qa.q: Why did Vidya ask if the teacher liked Jagdish more?
qa.a: She feared she was losing her special place and the teacher's attention to a new rival.

qa.q: How could Vidya's mother help her with this feeling?
qa.a: She could listen, name that it is hard to share attention, and remind Vidya that the teacher still noticed her energy.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel if he noticed Vidya's stiff smile?
qa.a: He might feel awkward or unwelcome, unsure why she is cold towards him.

grounding: Shows a child's jealousy about losing a teacher's attention and status to a new peer, in a community centre.

passage: I'm Vinita, and I sit two rows behind Darshan in Class 6. He and Kunal have been best friends since Class 1. Then a new boy joined in July, and Kunal started sharing his tiffin with him. Darshan stopped eating his own lunch. Yesterday, when Kunal laughed at the new boy's joke, Darshan got up and left the bench. Today he told Kunal, loudly, that the new boy "copies everything." I can't know what he feels inside, but he keeps watching the two of them.

qa.q: When did the new boy join?
qa.a: In July.

qa.q: What might Darshan be feeling when he watches Kunal and the new boy?
qa.a: He seems jealous and afraid of losing his best friend to the newcomer.

qa.q: What would you advise Darshan to try instead of calling the new boy a copier?
qa.a: Tell Kunal honestly that he misses him, and try including the new boy rather than pushing him away.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Darshan's behaviour?
qa.a: Kunal may feel confused and hurt that his best friend is acting cold for no clear reason.

grounding: Shows a child fearing that a new classmate will take his best friend's place, seen by a classmate.

passage: The first week after her baby brother Thomas came home, Anjali, ten, watched relatives crowd round his cot. Nobody asked about her science prize. She slammed her door. The next Sunday, when Amma asked her to hold Thomas for a photo, she said, "Why? Everyone only cares about him." Two weeks later Amma sat with her alone and asked about the prize. Anjali talked for twenty minutes. That evening she held Thomas while Amma cooked, and he grabbed her finger.

qa.q: What prize had Anjali won?
qa.a: Her science prize.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she said "Everyone only cares about him"?
qa.a: She felt jealous and hurt, afraid her baby brother had taken all the attention.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She made time for Anjali alone and asked about the prize, so Anjali felt she still mattered.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to hear Anjali's words?
qa.a: It is probably painful and worrying, which pushes her to give Anjali time alone.

grounding: Shows a child's jealousy when a new baby takes family attention, easing when her mother makes time for her.

passage: "You think you're the only one who's felt this? When I, your Harish Dadu, was nine, my best friend was Sumit. We walked to school together every day. Then a boy from Bombay came, with a shiny compass box and stories about the sea. Sumit started walking with him. I was so afraid of losing Sumit that I told the teacher the new boy had broken my ruler. He hadn't. The teacher found out. That evening Sumit came to my house and said, 'You could have just walked with both of us.' So the next day, I did."

qa.q: What did the boy from Bombay have?
qa.a: A shiny compass box and stories about the sea.

qa.q: What was young Harish feeling when he lied to the teacher?
qa.a: He was jealous and afraid of losing Sumit to the new boy.

qa.q: What turning point in the story fixed things?
qa.a: Sumit coming to Harish's house and suggesting they all walk together.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Harish lied about the new boy?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and a bit angry, but he still wanted to keep his old friend.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child his fear of losing a friend to a newcomer led to a lie, and how the friend repaired things.

passage: The rain was so heavy after school in Nagpur that only one shared auto came, with space for two in the back. Jasleen climbed in and patted the seat next to her, but Mehak, the new girl, slid in first. Sonali had to squeeze in front beside the driver. All the way home she could hear them laughing about the art project they were doing together. Sonali stared at the wet windscreen. Every day this week it had been Mehak, Mehak, Mehak. What if Jasleen didn't need her anymore? When the auto stopped, Jasleen leaned forward. "Sonu, you're coming for the project tomorrow, na?" Sonali's throat was tight. "You have Mehak now." Jasleen blinked. "I have both of you, silly."

qa.q: Who slid into the seat beside Jasleen?
qa.a: Mehak, the new girl.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid of as she stared at the wet windscreen?
qa.a: She was scared and jealous, fearing Jasleen would like Mehak more and no longer need her.

qa.q: What could Sonali do now that Jasleen has invited her?
qa.a: She could go to the project tomorrow and try to get to know Mehak, and tell Jasleen honestly that she had felt left out.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Sonali's comment "You have Mehak now"?
qa.a: Jasleen seems surprised, since she thinks of both girls as her friends and hadn't noticed Sonali feeling left out.

grounding: In a crowded auto on a rainy day, a girl fears losing her best friend to a new classmate.

passage: Every day after school in Salt Lake, Elizabeth and Rhea walked home together. This week Rhea kept going up to Sharmila's flat instead, because Sharmila had a keyboard and was teaching her songs. On Thursday Elizabeth waited at the gate for ten minutes. Rhea ran past, waving. "Going to Sharmila's!" Elizabeth kicked a stone all the way home. At dinner she pushed her rice around. "Rhea's got a new best friend," she said finally. "Sharmila can play music. I can't do anything like that." Her mother put a hand on hers. "Did Rhea say that?" Elizabeth shook her head slowly.

qa.q: What did Sharmila have that Rhea liked?
qa.a: A keyboard, and she was teaching Rhea songs.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she kicked a stone all the way home?
qa.a: She felt jealous and hurt, worried she was losing Rhea to Sharmila.

qa.q: How could Elizabeth's mother help her with this feeling?
qa.a: She could help Elizabeth ask Rhea directly, or suggest inviting Rhea over for something they both enjoy.

qa.q: How might Rhea see her time at Sharmila's?
qa.a: Rhea may just be excited about the music and not realise that Elizabeth feels left behind.

grounding: A girl fears losing her friend's attention to a peer who teaches music.

passage:
"Dolma, why are you slamming things?"
"I'm not."
Seema Didi raised an eyebrow. "You threw your bag at the wall."
Dolma flopped onto the bed. "Pema sat with the new girl at lunch. Again."
"So?"
"So she's always with Yangchen now. They laugh at jokes I don't even get."
"Did Pema stop talking to you?"
"...No. But she will."
"Ah." Seema sat down. "You're scared you'll lose her."
Dolma hugged her pillow. "Maybe."
"What if you sat with both of them tomorrow?"
"What if they don't want me?"
"What if they do?"

qa.q: What did Dolma throw at the wall?
qa.a: Her bag.

qa.q: What does Dolma's "No. But she will" show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she is jealous and anxious, fearing she will lose Pema even though it hasn't happened yet.

qa.q: What small step did Seema Didi suggest?
qa.a: Sitting with both Pema and Yangchen tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Pema see things if she knew how Dolma felt?
qa.a: Pema might be surprised, since she hasn't stopped talking to Dolma, and could reassure her.

grounding: At home, a girl admits to her older sister that she fears losing her friend to a new girl.

passage:
In Class 5, Farida was my best friend. We sat together, shared tiffin, walked home together every day.

Then a new girl, Rhea, joined. Farida started sitting with her at lunch. They laughed at jokes I didn't get.

I felt sick every lunchtime. I kept thinking Farida would forget me. I even said something mean about Rhea's bag, which I'm not proud of.

One day Farida asked, "Why are you so grumpy?" I told her the truth: "I'm scared you like her more."

She laughed and hugged me. "I can have two friends, silly."

I'm Charu, and the three of us ate together after that.

qa.q: What did Charu say about Rhea's bag?
qa.a: Charu said something mean about Rhea's bag.

qa.q: What was Charu afraid of when Farida sat with Rhea?
qa.a: Charu felt jealous and scared, afraid of losing Farida to the new girl.

qa.q: What helped Charu handle the jealousy?
qa.a: Telling Farida the truth about the fear, instead of staying grumpy, let them talk it through.

qa.q: How might Rhea have felt when Charu was mean about her bag?
qa.a: Rhea may have felt hurt or confused, not knowing why Charu disliked her.

grounding: A child looks back on feeling jealous when a best friend grew close to a new girl, and talking about the fear.

passage:
Teacher's note, Christmas term.

Sarita and Meenu have been best friends all year. For the Christmas carol duet, Meenu chose Tina as her partner instead of Sarita.

Sarita went very quiet. At break she snapped at Tina and told Meenu, "Fine, go sing with her." Later she cried in the corridor. She said, "Meenu will like Tina more now."

I sat with her and said it's normal to feel scared of losing a friend. I suggested she tell Meenu how she felt. She did at lunch. Meenu said the duet was only because Tina's voice matched hers.

— Hansa

qa.q: Who did Meenu choose for the duet?
qa.a: Meenu chose Tina as her partner.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she snapped at Tina?
qa.a: Sarita was jealous and afraid of losing Meenu's friendship to Tina.

qa.q: How did Hansa help Sarita with her jealousy?
qa.a: Hansa sat with her, said the fear was normal, and suggested talking honestly to Meenu.

qa.q: How might Tina have felt when Sarita snapped at her?
qa.a: Tina may have felt hurt or confused, since she only sang with Meenu for the duet.

grounding: A teacher notes a child's jealousy when her best friend picks another partner, and helps her talk about it.

passage:
Onam, Sunday

Aadhya came from Dubai for Onam, and suddenly Ammachi only talks to her. Aadhya helped make the pookalam. Aadhya sang the song. Aadhya got the first payasam.

I've been Ammachi's favourite since forever. She always calls me her "kutti". Today she didn't call me that even once.

I went and sat on the back steps and didn't come for the sadya until Amma called twice.

Then Ammachi came out and sat next to me. "Thomas, Aadhya is here for ten days. You're here every day." She gave me a whole banana chip packet.

I still feel a bit weird. But less.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya come from?
qa.a: Aadhya came from Dubai for Onam.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Ammachi paid attention to Aadhya?
qa.a: Thomas felt jealous and hurt, afraid of losing the place as Ammachi's favourite.

qa.q: How did Ammachi help Thomas?
qa.a: She came and sat with Thomas and reassured that their bond stays, since Thomas is there every day.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel if she knew Thomas was upset?
qa.a: Aadhya might feel surprised or sorry, since she was only enjoying her short visit.

grounding: During Onam, a child feels jealous when a visiting cousin gets the grandmother's attention, and is reassured.

passage: All through Navratri, Vasudha and Sharmila had practised garba steps behind the village temple. On the fifth evening a new girl, Kamala, arrived from the city with a mirror-work skirt and quick feet. Sharmila laughed at her jokes and learned her twirl. Vasudha stood at the edge, pulling at her dupatta. When Sharmila called, "Vasu, come, Kamala's teaching us!", Vasudha said she had a headache and walked home the long way. At the gate she stopped, eyes stinging. "She'll pair with Kamala for the final night," she muttered. Next morning Sharmila turned up with two glass bangles. "One each for the last night, Vasu. You're my partner."

qa.q: What did Sharmila bring the next morning?
qa.a: She brought two glass bangles, one each for the last night.

qa.q: What was Vasudha afraid of when she walked home the long way?
qa.a: She was jealous and afraid that Sharmila would choose Kamala as her partner for the final night.

qa.q: What could Vasudha have tried instead of leaving?
qa.a: She could have joined the lesson and later told Sharmila honestly that she felt a bit left out.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen Vasudha's headache excuse?
qa.a: Sharmila may have sensed Vasudha was upset, which is why she came with the bangles to reassure her.

grounding: Shows a child's fear of losing her best friend to a newcomer during a festival.
